newsitem.title: UK: New Labour, old worries for London traders.
newsitem.headline: New Labour, old worries for London traders.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party may have convinced some of London's financial community its tax-and-spend days are over but traders on the floor of the City's busiest exchange are still unsure.

Talking to some of the 2,000 traders who work at London's International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) revealed strong support for the beleaguered Conservative Party and distrust of recent polls showing Labour cruising to victory.

"You can't trust the polls," said a trader at a U.S. Securities house. "People in the street are proud to say they're voting Labour, but embarassed about being Conservative. It's a different matter when they get into the voting booth."
The latest opinion polls showed the opposition Labour Party heading for victory on May 1, with a hefty lead of more that 21 percentage points over the ruling Conservatives.
But the polls were wrong in 1992, as several brightly-jacketed traders of British interest rate futures were keen to point out, and they could be wrong again.
"You expect big swings in the polls," said one. "The Tories will make a comeback. They always do."
Many of the traders interviewed thought that Labour's majority would be slim, with some suggesting there would be a hung parliament -- a situation in which no single party gains an overall majority.
But most of the anti-Labour feeling expressed around the pits and booths was focussed on personal issues such as tax, rather than issues of economic policy.
"I'm not voting for them because I don't want to pay 60 percent tax," said the manager of floor operations at a major bank. "They'll really hammer us on capital gains tax as well."
"And what's to stop them putting national insurance up ?" she said.
The average age on the (LIFFE) floor is 25-1/2, with basic salaries starting at 30,000 to 40,000 stg plus bonuses on top, well above the British national average salary of 20,000 stg.

There was great scorn for new Labour's less blue collar image, typified by Tony Blair. After 18 years in opposition, traders said Labour would not have the necessary experience and professionalism to govern well.

"Voters don't want the sort of people who wear button-down collars in government," said the manager of futures and options trading at a U.S. bank, referring to the casual attire favoured by many in the Labour Party.

From an economic viewpoint, many traders said Britain was in good shape compared with its European neighbours, and a Labour victory, they said, could mean a return to trade union power and constant strikes.

"People have forgotten what it was really like under Labour," said a 23-year old British government debt trader. "They've forgotten the rubbish rotting in the streets, and the dead left unburied because the gravediggers were on strike."
Although volatility -- which tends to rise when markets are concerned that large price movements are imminent -- has remained muted, traders said it would creep up over the next few weeks.

Some of the older traders were less concerned about the idea of a Labour government. Since Labour has stripped itself of some of its more left-wing policies, they said it was not radically different from the Conservatives.

"Their economic policies are quite similar," said a Bund trader. "Labour won't issue debt hand over fist, which was always the worry before, and they know they won't get away with high taxing and spending."
An Italian debt trader agreed, pinning voter-confidence this time, compared with the last election in 1992, on leadership.
"The difference this time is Blair. (Former Labour leader Neil) Kinnock was so over confident and so self-important," he said.
But asked whether they were sufficiently confident to put money on a Conservative victory, no-one was prepared to take up the challenge.
"I'd put a bet on there being a hung parliament," volunteered a trader at a U.S. bank. "Well, a small one anyway."
